title: Glycogen: the small tank that sets the limit
goal: Explain how much glycogen muscle and liver hold, how fast exercise drains it and why that brings fatigue, and how classic and modern carbohydrate loading fill it before a long race.

steps.title: Two stores, two jobs
steps.text:
An adult stores [glycogen](g:glycogen) in two places [[c:gly-amounts]]. At about 17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram:

| store | glycogen | energy |
|---|---|---|
| all skeletal muscle | about 400 g | about 6,800 kJ (1,600 kcal) |
| liver | about 80–100 g | about 1,360–1,700 kJ (320–400 kcal) |
| blood glucose | about 4–5 g | under 100 kJ |

The jobs differ. Muscle cells break down their own glycogen and burn the glucose themselves [[c:gly-muscle-own]]. The liver releases its glucose into the blood to keep blood glucose steady for the brain and working muscles [[c:gly-liver-job]].

[Muscle biopsies](g:muscle-biopsy) report it per kg of muscle: in trained, well-fed athletes after rest about **150 mmol·kg⁻¹ wet muscle**, up to about 200 after a few high-carbohydrate days, and below 50 after long hard exercise [[c:gly-concentration]].

claims.text: The body stores about 400 g of glycogen in muscle and about 100 g in the liver, with about 5 g of glucose in the blood.

evidence.quote: as glycogen in both the liver (approximately 100 g) and muscle (approximately 400 g) with 5 g also circulating in the blood stream as glucose
The > 80 g of glucose stored as liver glycogen is used to constantly replenish the 4 g of glucose circulating in the blood.

claims.text: Muscle glycogen is broken down to glucose that the same muscle cells oxidise to make ATP.

evidence.quote: muscle glycogen particles are broken down, freeing glucose molecules that muscle cells then oxidize through anaerobic and aerobic processes to produce the adenosine triphosphate (ATP) molecules required for muscle contraction

claims.text: Liver glycogen is released as glucose to keep blood glucose steady, which the brain depends on.

evidence.quote: To ensure the brain has an ample supply of glucose, the liver releases glucose into the bloodstream at a rate similar to the uptake of glucose from the blood into tissues, thereby stabilizing blood glucose concentration between 4.0 and 5.5 mmol/L (70–100 mg/dL).

claims.text: In trained, well-fed endurance athletes muscle glycogen is about 150 mmol·kg⁻¹ wet muscle after rest, up to about 200 after a few high-carbohydrate days, and can fall below 50 after prolonged intense exercise.

evidence.quote: In trained and well-fed endurance athletes, muscle glycogen concentration is roughly 150 mmol/kg wet weight following at least 8–12 hours of rest but can reach supercompensated levels of 200 mmol/kg wet weight in highly fit, rested athletes after a few days on high-carbohydrate diets

steps.title: How fast the tank drains
steps.text:
The harder you go, the faster glycogen goes. Moving from 65% to 85% of [VO₂max](g:vo2max), muscle and liver glycogen breakdown and glucose uptake all rise, and carbohydrate becomes the main fuel [[c:gly-intensity]]. That is the [crossover](g:crossover-point) from tier 1, seen from the fuel tank.

How full you start matters too. Trained runners who had loaded their muscles used more glycogen per km in a 20.9 km run (about 5 mmol·kg⁻¹ wet per km) than when they had not (about 3) [[c:gly-start-use]]. A full tank is spent more freely.

So the time a store lasts depends on pace, on how full it was, and on how much carbohydrate you eat on the way.

claims.text: As intensity rises from 65% to 85% VO₂max, muscle and liver glycogen breakdown and glucose uptake increase and carbohydrate becomes the main fuel.

evidence.quote: As exercise intensity progresses from moderate (i.e., 65% VO 2max ) to high-intensity (85% VO 2max ), muscle glycogenolysis, liver glycogenolysis and glucose uptake increase such that CHO metabolism predominates
The rate at which muscle glycogen is degraded depends primarily upon the intensity of physical activity; the greater the exercise intensity, the greater the rate at which muscle glycogen is degraded.

claims.text: Runners who started a 20.9 km run with loaded muscles used more glycogen per km (about 5 vs 3 mmol·kg⁻¹ wet).

evidence.quote: The performance run in both trials A and B utilized significantly more glycogen than in trial C: 5.0 and 5.1 mmG/km vs. 3.1 mmG/km.

steps.title: How long would the stores last?
steps.problem: A cyclist rides hard, burning carbohydrate at 3 g·min⁻¹ and eating nothing. She starts with 400 g of muscle glycogen and 90 g of liver glycogen. Roughly how long until both are gone?
steps: Time = store ÷ rate. Units: g ÷ g·min⁻¹ = min. 490 ÷ 3 ≈ 163 min.

This is an upper limit. The 400 g sits in all her muscles, but only the leg muscles are working hard; glycogen in her arms and trunk can't help them. Her legs run low sooner, and fat oxidation and food on the way change the sums.

steps.title: Running low: the wall
steps.text:
The muscle biopsy studies of the late 1960s set the rules still used today: glycogen is used faster the harder you go, high-carbohydrate diets raise glycogen and lengthen how long you can keep going, and glycogen refills above normal after it has been run down [[c:gly-scandi]].

In efforts over about 90 minutes, exhaustion usually comes when muscle glycogen is critically low, around 25 mmol·kg⁻¹ wet, and burning more blood glucose can't make up for it [[c:gly-critical]]. Liver glycogen running out is a major cause of fatigue too, because blood glucose then falls ([hypoglycaemia](g:hypoglycaemia)) [[c:gly-depletion-fatigue]].

In marathons, the sudden late slowdown is [hitting the wall](g:hitting-the-wall); one analysis puts it at more than two in five runners [[c:wall-common]]. *Fatigue in long efforts* covers why an emptying muscle weakens.

claims.text: Biopsy studies showed that glycogen use depends on intensity, that high-carbohydrate diets raise glycogen and exercise capacity, and that glycogen refills above normal after depletion.

evidence.quote: These researchers provided the platform for modern day sports nutrition practice in a series of studies that collectively demonstrated that (1) muscle glycogen is depleted during exercise in an intensity dependent manner; (2) high CHO diets increase muscle glycogen storage and subsequently improve exercise capacity and (3) muscle glycogen storage is acutely enhanced following prior glycogen depletion (i.e., the super-compensation effect)

claims.text: In endurance events over 90 min, exhaustion usually coincides with critically low muscle glycogen (about 25 mmol·kg⁻¹ wet).

evidence.quote: During this type of exercise, exhaustion usually coincides with critically low (25 mmol/kg wet weight) muscle glycogen contents, suggesting the supply of energy from glycogen utilisation cannot be replaced by an increased oxidation of blood glucose.

claims.text: Depletion of both muscle and liver glycogen is a major cause of fatigue in endurance exercise.

evidence.quote: it follows that glycogen depletion (in both muscle and liver) is a major cause of fatigue in both endurance and high-intensity (intermittent) type activities
As such, it is now generally accepted that liver glycogen depletion is also a major contributing cause of fatigue during endurance exercise.

claims.text: More than two in five marathon runners experience performance-limiting carbohydrate depletion ('hitting the wall').

evidence.quote: more than two-fifths experience severe and performance-limiting depletion of physiologic carbohydrate reserves (a phenomenon known as 'hitting the wall')

steps.title: Carbohydrate loading: classic and modern
steps.text:
[Carbohydrate loading](g:carbohydrate-loading) fills muscle glycogen above its usual level before a long race.

| protocol | what you do |
|---|---|
| classic (1960s) | 3 days hard training, low carbohydrate (under 5 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹), then 3 days of [taper](g:taper), high carbohydrate |
| modified (Sherman, 1981) | 3-day taper, high carbohydrate, no depletion |
| short (Bussau, 2002) | 1 day of about 10 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹, resting |

The classic version worked, but its low-carbohydrate days were very hard [[c:load-classic]]. Without depletion, runners reached about the same glycogen [[c:load-sherman]]. Eight trained men resting on 10 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ went from 95 to 180 mmol·kg⁻¹ wet in one day, then no higher [[c:load-1day]]. Today's advice: 10–12 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for 36–48 h [[c:load-modern]]. Each gram of glycogen holds at least 3 g of water, so the scales show a little more [[c:gly-water]].

claims.text: Classic loading (3 days of hard training on low carbohydrate, then 3 days of taper on high carbohydrate) supercompensates glycogen but makes training very hard; a 3-day high-carbohydrate taper without depletion reaches similar stores.

evidence.quote: Classic glycogen loading: 3 d of hard training on a low-CHO diet (<5 g/kg BW/d) followed by 3 d of tapered training on a high-CHO diet Supercompensated muscle glycogen stores compared with before the intervention but training is very difficult both physically and psychologically during the low-CHO phase
Modified glycogen loading: 3-d taper on a high-CHO diet with 24-h rest prior to competitions Supercompensated muscle glycogen stores similar to the classic loading regimen

claims.text: A moderate taper-and-diet regimen without a low-carbohydrate depletion phase raised muscle glycogen as much as the regimen with depletion.

evidence.quote: Trials A, B, and C elevated muscle glycogen to 207, 203, and 159 mmol glucosyl units/kg wet tissue (mmG), respectively.
These data demonstrate that (1) muscle glycogen can be elevated to high levels with a moderate exercise-diet regimen

claims.text: In 8 trained men who rested and ate 10 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ of carbohydrate, muscle glycogen reached its maximum (95 to 180 mmol·kg⁻¹ wet) after 1 day.

evidence.quote: Muscle glycogen content increased significantly ( P<0.05) from pre-loading levels of [mean (SE)] 95 (5) to 180 (15) mmol.kg(-1) wet mass after only 1 day, and remained stable afterwards despite another 2 days of carbohydrate-rich diet.

claims.text: For events over 90 min, loading in the 36–48 h before may improve performance by 2–3%; 1 day of 10–12 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ after short exercise or rest supercompensates glycogen.

evidence.quote: For events lasting >90 min however, glycogen supercompensation, or “carbo loading,” in the preceding 36–48 h may help improve performance by 2–3%

However recent studies show that short-term high-intensity exercise (or even complete physical inactivity) followed by a 1-day high (10–12 g/kg/day) intake of CHO similarly achieves glycogen supercompensation, and this is maintained for 3 days

claims.text: Each gram of glycogen is stored with at least 3 g of water, so loading adds body mass.

evidence.quote: Each gram of glycogen is stored with at least 3 g of water, 14 , 15 making weight gain a noticeable response to glycogen super-compensation in many athletes.

steps.title: Who gains from loading?
steps.text:
Loading only pays when the race is long enough to run the tank low [[c:load-benefit]]:

| event | effect of more starting glycogen |
|---|---|
| all-out, under 5 min | little or none |
| 60–90 min at moderate pace | none: glycogen is left over at the finish |
| over 90 min, to exhaustion | fatigue about 20% later |
| over 90 min, set distance | about 2–3% faster |

In trained runners, loading didn't change 20.9 km times [[c:load-no-21k]].

So: marathon, Ironman, a long road race or gran fondo, yes. A 10 km run, a 40 km time trial or a sprint triathlon need a normal high-carbohydrate day before, not a full load. And the water stored with the extra glycogen is a small cost, even on a hilly course.

claims.text: Raising starting glycogen doesn't help all-out efforts under 5 min or moderate exercise of 60–90 min, but delays fatigue by about 20% in events over 90 min and improves set-distance performance by 2–3%.

evidence.quote: This review suggests that there is little or no effect of elevating pre-exercise muscle glycogen contents above normal resting values on a single exhaustive bout of high-intensity exercise lasting less than 5 minutes. Nor is there any benefit of increasing starting muscle glycogen content on moderate-intensity running or cycling lasting 60 to 90 minutes.
However, elevated starting muscle glycogen content will postpone fatigue by approximately equal to 20% in endurance events lasting more than 90 minutes.
In such exercise, high carbohydrate diets have been reported to improve performance by 2 to 3%.

claims.text: Carbohydrate loading did not improve performance of trained runners over 20.9 km.

evidence.quote: (3) carbohydrate loading is of no benefit to performance for trained runners during a 20.9-km run.

points: Muscle holds about 400 g of glycogen (about 6,800 kJ) for its own use; the liver holds 80–100 g and keeps blood glucose up.
Glycogen drains faster at higher intensity, and faster when you start full.
In efforts over 90 min, critically low muscle glycogen and falling liver glycogen bring fatigue: the wall.
Loading has gone from 6 punishing days to 36–48 h of 10–12 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ with little training.
Load for events over 90 min (about 2–3% faster); shorter races need only a normal high-carbohydrate day.

variants.stem: Late in a long fasted ride, a cyclist's leg muscles still hold some glycogen, yet his blood glucose is falling and he feels foggy. What explains this?

options.text: Muscle glycogen fuels the muscle that stores it; blood glucose depends on the liver
options.why: Right: muscle cells burn their own glycogen; it is the liver that tops up the blood, and its small store is running low.

options.text: The legs release their glycogen into the blood only after the liver is empty
options.why: Muscle doesn't hand its glycogen to the blood as glucose; it uses it itself.

options.text: Blood glucose is falling because the brain stores glucose as glycogen during exercise
options.why: The brain holds only a tiny amount of glycogen; the fall comes from the liver's output not keeping up.

options.text: Blood glucose is falling because fat oxidation turns glucose into fat
options.why: Burning fat doesn't convert blood glucose into fat; the liver's supply is the issue.

variants.stem: A runner's liver holds 90 g of glycogen. At about 17 kJ per gram, how much energy is that?

options.text: About 1,530 kJ
options.why: Right: 90 × 17 = 1,530 kJ (about 360 kcal).

options.text: About 3,330 kJ
options.why: This uses 37 kJ per gram, the value for fat, not carbohydrate.

options.text: About 360 kJ
options.why: 360 is the answer in kcal (90 × 4), not kJ.

options.text: About 5.3 kJ
options.why: This divides 90 by 17 instead of multiplying.

variants.solution: Energy = mass × energy per gram = 90 g × 17 kJ·g⁻¹ = 1,530 kJ (90 × 4 = 360 kcal).

variants.stem: After loading, a triathlete's muscles hold about 600 g of glycogen. At about 17 kJ per gram, how much energy is that?

options.text: About 10,200 kJ
options.why: Right: 600 × 17 = 10,200 kJ (about 2,400 kcal).

options.text: About 22,200 kJ
options.why: This uses 37 kJ per gram, the value for fat, not carbohydrate.

options.text: About 2,400 kJ
options.why: 2,400 is the answer in kcal (600 × 4), not kJ.

options.text: About 35 kJ
options.why: This divides 600 by 17 instead of multiplying.

variants.solution: Energy = mass × energy per gram = 600 g × 17 kJ·g⁻¹ = 10,200 kJ (600 × 4 = 2,400 kcal).

variants.stem: The same rider does two 90-min rides: one at 65% of VO₂max, one at 85%. What happens to her muscle glycogen?

options.text: It falls faster in the 85% ride
options.why: Right: glycogen breakdown rises with intensity, and carbohydrate becomes the main fuel.

options.text: It falls at the same rate, as both last 90 min
options.why: Duration is the same, but the rate of use depends mainly on intensity.

options.text: It falls faster in the 65% ride
options.why: At 65% more fat is used; at 85% carbohydrate use, and so glycogen breakdown, is higher.

options.text: It doesn't fall in either ride
options.why: Muscle glycogen is a major fuel at both intensities.

variants.stem: A marathoner burns carbohydrate at 2.5 g·min⁻¹ and eats nothing. He starts with 380 g of muscle glycogen and 70 g of liver glycogen. Roughly how long until both are gone?

options.text: About 180 min
options.why: Right: (380 + 70) ÷ 2.5 = 450 ÷ 2.5 = 180 min, an upper limit.

options.text: About 152 min
options.why: This uses the muscle store only (380 ÷ 2.5) and forgets the liver.

options.text: About 1,125 min
options.why: This multiplies store by rate (450 × 2.5); time = store ÷ rate.

options.text: About 3 min
options.why: This gives the answer in hours (180 ÷ 60 = 3) but labels it minutes.

variants.solution: Stores = 380 + 70 = 450 g. Time = 450 g ÷ 2.5 g·min⁻¹ = 180 min (3 h). An upper limit: not all muscle glycogen is in the working legs.

variants.stem: A triathlete on the bike burns carbohydrate at 2 g·min⁻¹ and eats nothing. She starts with 360 g of muscle glycogen and 80 g of liver glycogen. Roughly how long until both are gone?

options.text: About 220 min
options.why: Right: (360 + 80) ÷ 2 = 440 ÷ 2 = 220 min, an upper limit.

options.text: About 180 min
options.why: This uses the muscle store only (360 ÷ 2) and forgets the liver.

options.text: About 880 min
options.why: This multiplies store by rate (440 × 2); time = store ÷ rate.

options.text: About 3.7 min
options.why: This gives the answer in hours (220 ÷ 60 ≈ 3.7) but labels it minutes.

variants.solution: Stores = 360 + 80 = 440 g. Time = 440 g ÷ 2 g·min⁻¹ = 220 min (about 3.7 h). An upper limit: not all muscle glycogen is in the working legs.

variants.stem: A cyclist in a hard road race burns carbohydrate at 4 g·min⁻¹ and eats nothing. He starts with 420 g of muscle glycogen and 100 g of liver glycogen. Roughly how long until both are gone?

options.text: About 130 min
options.why: Right: (420 + 100) ÷ 4 = 520 ÷ 4 = 130 min, an upper limit.

options.text: About 105 min
options.why: This uses the muscle store only (420 ÷ 4) and forgets the liver.

options.text: About 2,080 min
options.why: This multiplies store by rate (520 × 4); time = store ÷ rate.

options.text: About 2.2 min
options.why: This gives the answer in hours (130 ÷ 60 ≈ 2.2) but labels it minutes.

variants.solution: Stores = 420 + 100 = 520 g. Time = 520 g ÷ 4 g·min⁻¹ = 130 min (about 2.2 h). An upper limit: not all muscle glycogen is in the working legs.

variants.stem: A runner's sums say her glycogen should last 3 h, but she fades badly at 2 h 20 min with nothing eaten. Which flaw in the sums best explains the gap?

options.text: Glycogen in her arms and trunk can't fuel her legs, so the legs run low first
options.why: Right: each muscle burns its own glycogen, so the working legs empty before the whole-body total does.

options.text: Her liver glycogen is held back for after the race
options.why: The liver releases glucose throughout exercise; it doesn't keep a reserve for later.

options.text: She burned more fat than expected, which uses up glycogen faster
options.why: Burning more fat spares glycogen; it doesn't speed its use.

options.text: Glycogen gives more energy per gram than the 17 kJ in the sums
options.why: If anything, a higher energy value would make the stores last longer, not shorter.

variants.stem: At 32 km of a marathon, a runner who ate little before or during the race slows sharply, though she isn't overheating and her breathing feels easy. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Muscle and liver glycogen have run critically low
options.why: Right: this late, sudden slowdown fits hitting the wall from low carbohydrate stores.

options.text: Lactate has built up from running above her threshold
options.why: Marathon pace is below the threshold for most runners, and her easy breathing argues against it.

options.text: Her phosphocreatine stores have run out
options.why: PCr matters for seconds-long efforts and recovers quickly; it doesn't cause a slowdown after 2–3 h.

options.text: Her fat stores have run out
options.why: Even a lean runner holds enough fat for days; it is the carbohydrate store that empties.

variants.stem: What is today's usual carbohydrate-loading advice before an event lasting over 90 minutes?

options.text: 10–12 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for 36–48 h, training little
options.why: Right: a day or two of high carbohydrate with reduced training fills muscle glycogen.

options.text: 3 days low carbohydrate, then 3 days high carbohydrate
options.why: That is the classic 1960s protocol, now dropped because the depletion phase is hard and unnecessary.

options.text: 5–7 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ for a week, training as usual
options.why: That is an everyday intake for moderate training; it won't fill glycogen above normal.

options.text: A large pasta meal the night before only
options.why: One meal rarely supplies 10–12 g·kg⁻¹ over a full day; loading needs high intake across 1–2 days.

variants.stem: Why have coaches largely dropped the classic loading protocol with its 3 low-carbohydrate days of hard training?

options.text: A high-carbohydrate taper alone fills glycogen about as well
options.why: Right: the modified regimen reached similar glycogen levels and spares athletes the punishing low-carbohydrate phase.

options.text: It never raised muscle glycogen above normal levels
options.why: It did supercompensate glycogen; the problem was the cost, not the effect.

options.text: It was shown to make performance worse over 20 km
options.why: Loading didn't help a 20.9 km run, but it didn't harm it either; that isn't why the depletion phase was dropped.

options.text: It only works in untrained people
options.why: Trained athletes supercompensate too; the 1-day protocol was tested in trained men.

variants.stem: The 1-day loading study gave 8 trained men 10 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ while they rested, and measured muscle glycogen by biopsy. What most limits its use as advice for a female triathlete before an Ironman?

options.text: Only 8 men were tested, and performance was never measured
options.why: Right: a small, all-male sample, and it shows glycogen went up, not that racing got better.

options.text: Biopsies can't measure muscle glycogen
options.why: Biopsies are the standard way to measure muscle glycogen.

options.text: The men were trained, so the result is too strong
options.why: Trained athletes are the right group for this question; that is a strength, not a limit.

options.text: The study lasted 3 days, too long to judge a 1-day protocol
options.why: The extra days showed glycogen didn't keep rising, which supports the 1-day result.

variants.stem: A runner plans a full 2-day carbohydrate load before a 10 km race she expects to finish in 42 min. What is the best judgement?

options.text: Unneeded: glycogen won't run low in 42 min, so a normal high-carbohydrate day will do
options.why: Right: extra glycogen gives no benefit in efforts under 90 min, and the added water weight is a small cost.

options.text: Wise: loading improves every race by 2–3%
options.why: The 2–3% gain applies to events over 90 min, not a 42-min race.

options.text: Wise, but only with a low-carbohydrate depletion phase first
options.why: The depletion phase isn't needed even when loading makes sense, and here loading itself isn't needed.

options.text: Harmful: high carbohydrate before short races lowers glycogen
options.why: Eating more carbohydrate doesn't lower glycogen; it just gives no benefit here.

variants.stem: A triathlete expects to finish an Ironman in about 11 h. Should he load carbohydrate in the 36–48 h before?

options.text: Yes: in events over 90 min, fuller glycogen improves performance
options.why: Right: for events over 90 min, higher starting glycogen delays fatigue and improves set-distance performance by about 2–3%.

options.text: No: Ironman pace is so easy that it runs on fat alone
options.why: Even at Ironman pace carbohydrate is a major fuel, and over 11 h the stores run low.

options.text: No: eating during the race makes the starting stores irrelevant
options.why: Race feeding helps a lot, but the gut can't replace all the carbohydrate burned; starting full still matters.

options.text: Only with 3 days of low-carbohydrate training first
options.why: The depletion phase is not needed; 1–2 days of high intake fills glycogen.
